01: If a stretch of the file happens to equal a repeated-digit number (like 1111 in base 2 or 7777 in base 10), we can store the recipe instead of the bytes. How long must such a stretch be before recipe + position + length is shorter than the bytes themselves?

The encoder scans the file for stretches that equal a repdigit or a ratio of two repdigits, and chooses where each stretch starts and ends to minimise the total. Everything not covered is stored literally.
02: Can a number that is *almost* a product of two smaller numbers be stored as the two factors plus a small correction? Does writing a factor's digits side by side make it cheaper?

For each block the encoder looks for a nearby value that factors well, then stores the factors and the signed difference. A variant splits a large factor into decimal digit groups and recurses into them.
03: Can a block be written as the output of a simple generator (a power, or a sum of seeded pseudo-random numbers) plus an exact correction?
The encoder tries a fixed budget of seeds or exponents, keeps the candidate closest to the block, and stores the choice plus the additive or XOR correction.
04: Can digits of sums of square roots (like √2 − √3 + √5) reproduce pieces of a file, with occasional restarts when they stop matching?
The encoder searches signed sums of up to four square roots, certifies how many digits match, and stores the coefficients plus checkpoint positions where a new sum takes over.
05: Every number can be written in any base. Is there a base in which a block has a few dominant digits, so that storing the base plus the exceptions is shorter?

Per file or per block, the encoder picks a base from 2 to 257, codes the dominant digits cheaply and lists the exceptional digits. It compares choosing the base by entropy with choosing it by actual encoded size.
06: A reversible cellular automaton can be run backwards. If a grid looks like the result of many automaton steps, is it cheaper to store the earlier, simpler grid plus the number of steps?
For each small bit grid the encoder runs checkerboard or Margolus rules backwards, keeps the state that is cheapest to code, and stores it with the step count (fixed, limited or searched).
07: Does running an automaton backwards before factoring a bit matrix make the matrix easier to factor, and does factoring the factors again help?
Each 16×16 bit matrix is optionally evolved backwards, then written as basis rows times coefficient rows plus an error mask, recursively up to three levels.
08: A bit matrix written as U × V plus errors has many equally valid (U, V) pairs. Does picking the pair that is cheapest to store make the archive smaller?
The encoder fixes the rank and the error mask, then changes the factor basis to the version whose U and V cost fewest bits.
09: Can a few large Walsh–Hadamard (binary Fourier) coefficients predict each bit plane, so that only the coefficients and the wrong bits need storing?
Each bit plane is transformed, its largest coefficients are kept, and the plane they predict is XORed with the real one to give a sparse correction.
10: Our own lab produced long lists of 'multiply by a, add b' instructions. What is the most compact way to write that instruction stream, and how fast can it be replayed?
Three encodings of the (a, b) pairs are compared, including one byte for the most common multiplier, and two ways of replaying the chain (one step at a time or by balanced composition).
11: How often must a piece of an expression repeat before defining it once and referring to it pays off?
The same instruction listing is stored flat, as a sequence grammar (repeated runs become rules) or as a graph of shared subexpressions.
12: If the receiver already has a similar file (an older version), how small can the difference be made, and which way of describing the difference works best?
Three patch styles are compared: XOR at fixed offsets, copies from movable positions, and full alignment with insertions and deletions.
13: Does the Burrows–Wheeler transform (the reordering used by bzip2) make the data easier for a generator or a residual coder to predict?
The same predictors and the same residual coder run on the original bytes and on their BWT, so the effect of the reordering is isolated.
14: When most of a correction is zero, what is the cheapest way to store the few wrong positions: an exact combinatorial rank, gaps between them, or a context model?
The same sparse error masks are coded four ways, and a per-block selector picks the best.
15: Executables contain predictable parts (headers, tables, padding). Can a catalogue of generators recreate those parts of a real binary cheaply enough to pay for listing where they are?
The encoder rebuilds ELF headers from the file's own structure and scans for local formula matches; everything else is stored literally.
16: Is it worth switching between methods inside one file (for example a formula here, a copy there), once every switch is paid for?
The encoder compares one method for the whole file, a choice per fixed block, and a choice per variable interval found by dynamic programming.
formula-factor-grammar: Experiments 01, 02 and 11 combined: when a factor already has a short repdigit recipe, does a dictionary of shared factors still add anything?
Products hiding a repdigit factor are coded with factor leaves stored literally, as recipes, as shared recipes, or both.
automaton-factor-residual: Experiments 06, 07, 08 and 14 combined: with the factor model held fixed, does undoing an automaton step make the residual cheaper?
The same factorization and residual coder run with and without an automaton step in front, and with direct or enumerative residual coding.
reference-formula-intervals: Experiments 12, 15 and 16 combined: when a file mixes copies of a reference with generated stretches, does choosing between them per interval pay for the bookkeeping?
A per-interval selector chooses literal, reference copy or formula, and the result is compared with each method alone.
factor-trees: Read a big file as one integer. Can splitting it into factors and children, again and again, describe it in fewer bytes than the file?
Each node removes its small prime factors, then splits the remaining number into 2 to 128 children at chosen bit positions, keeping every width so the bytes can be rebuilt.
whiteboard-trees: Can the whiteboard formula (one repeated-digit number divided by another) describe nodes inside a factor tree, even if it cannot describe a whole file?
At each tree node the encoder looks for a scaled quotient of two repdigits; if none fits it splits the cofactor again.
shared-factor-forest: If several words of a file share the same factor and the same formula, can one stored recipe serve them all?
Words are divided, cofactors are cut at bit boundaries, children that match a repdigit quotient become formula leaves, and identical recipes are stored once in a shared table.
carry-trees: Does multiplying or dividing the whole file by a small number before splitting it expose regions that the same trick on each piece would miss?
The file is scaled (for example by 12), split into regions, and sparse arithmetic regions are coded while the rest stays literal; the order of scaling and splitting is compared.
prime-index-trees: Many words of a file are primes or products of primes. Is it cheaper to store a word as the index of its prime (the 1,000th prime) than as the word itself?
Words are replaced by prime ordinals or factor lists where that is shorter, with selectors marking which words were replaced.
integer-formulas: Can a whole file, read as one huge integer, be written as a sum of squares, a product of consecutive integers or a modular square, with a short remainder?
Greedy searches fit each formula family to the full integer and store the formula plus the exact remainder.
generator-sums: If we try 16.7 million triples of seeds, how much of a block can the sum of three pseudo-random numbers explain?
For every 4 KiB block the encoder searches seed triples whose summed outputs come closest, then stores three seed bytes and the signed residual.
whiteboard-census: How many numbers does the whiteboard formula actually shorten, and can its tables be rebuilt from the formula?
An exhaustive enumerator computes, for every number below 2ᴺ, the cheapest repdigit or repdigit ratio. Its tables and witness records are then compressed by recomputation, by columns, or both.
portable-arithmetic: The record archive Q contains an executable and neural-network weights. If we rebuild those parts from their structure, how much does Q shrink once the decoder program is counted too?
A self-contained Python package rebuilds Q: it regenerates the executable's tables and the model weights inside 12 × Q, stores the rest literally, and divides by 12.
repdigit-intervals: Do whiteboard-style repdigit numbers appear at useful positions inside the record archive Q?
Every byte offset is tried as the start of a repdigit or repdigit quotient; dynamic programming picks the set of non-overlapping replacements that saves most.
quartic-trees: Can Q be written as nested formulas of the form (a⁴ + d⁴) / 2ᵏ, recursing into a and d?
Each node solves for two operands whose fourth powers produce the target, then recurses into the operands until they are small.
hierarchical-gf2: Does running a cellular automaton backwards before factoring a bit matrix expose low rank that factoring alone misses?
Files are cut into 16×16 bit matrices; each matrix may be evolved backwards, then factored recursively as basis rows, coefficients and an error mask.
tensor-orbits: In three dimensions, can stepping a volume backwards through an automaton make its planes low rank, and therefore cheap?
The encoder evolves a 3-D volume backwards, stores the earlier state as low-rank panels plus corrections, and the decoder steps it forward again.
checkerboard-orbits: If many matrices lie on the same automaton orbit, is it cheaper to send one clock (step count) for a whole page than one per matrix? Separately: does a scanline XOR plus a tree of empty regions help scanned pages?
Matrices are evolved backwards with a shared or individual step count. For documents, each scanline is XORed with the one above and empty quadrants are skipped.
modular-kronecker: With byte-valued cells (arithmetic modulo 256), can reversing an automaton reveal that a panel is the product of two small 4×4 matrices?
Panels are evolved backwards, fitted as a Kronecker product of two small matrices, and the exact byte differences are stored.
four-dimensional-factors: In four dimensions (space plus time) with noise, can reversing an automaton recover a low-rank structure, and does the choice among equivalent factor bases change the size?
The encoder reverses the 4-D evolution, factors each block into two bit matrices plus an error matrix, and tries equivalent bases.
learned-cellular-rules: What if the automaton rule is unknown? Can it be learned from the data together with the way its errors are correlated?
Per bit plane the encoder learns a 32-entry rule table and a change of basis for the residual byte, either one after the other or jointly.
lattice-prediction: Many files are secretly tables: fixed-width records or grids of numbers. Can a decoder discover the row width and predict each value from its neighbours, and does that help a standard compressor?

A scan finds widths and strides where values repeat, numbers are predicted from the row above or the previous sample, bit planes are separated, and variable-length records are split into one stream per field before a standard back end.
distance-geometry: A table of distances between points is fully determined by the points' positions. Can a decoder rebuild the whole table from a few landmark columns?

The encoder picks three or four well-spread landmarks, stores their full distance columns, recovers each point's coordinates relative to them, predicts every other distance and stores the exact errors.
shape-context: A fax page is a grid of black and white pixels. Can a model that finds the row width and predicts each pixel from its neighbours beat the fax standards?
The coder detects the row width, then range-codes each bit with a context made of nearby pixels in the same and previous rows.
glyph-residuals: Scanned manuals are printed from a few hundred letter shapes. Can storing each shape once, plus where it appears and an exact pixel correction, beat DjVu and JBIG?
Connected components are extracted, similar ones share one stored bitmap, their positions are coded, and an exact residual fixes every pixel that differs.
text-views: Does normalising spelling and XML fields before the Burrows–Wheeler transform make Wikipedia text easier to compress?
Reversible views (capital flags, field normalisation, BWT, move-to-front) are applied and the result is compressed by a standard back end.
arithmetic-references: If the receiver already owns a related file (a previous release, or the record archive), how small can a patch be, and what does it cost if the reference has to be sent too?
The new file is coded relative to the reference with copies and arithmetic transforms; sizes are reported with and without delivering the reference.
reversible-wavelets: Does a reversible colour transform followed by an integer wavelet compress photos better than PNG, WebP or JPEG XL?
RGB is converted to reversible colour-difference planes, each plane goes through a multi-level integer wavelet, and coefficients are context-coded.
motion-residuals: In video, does storing a motion vector per block improve prediction enough to pay for itself?
Each frame is predicted from the previous one with or without per-block motion and from spatial neighbours, and the residual is coded.
wiki-structures: Wikipedia pages share templates and structure. Does grouping similar pages, or priming the compressor with typical page text, help?
Pages are reordered or split into template slots, then compressed with xz or with several CM3 members primed with similar text.
context-mixer: How well can a context-mixing compressor written from scratch in this project compress English Wikipedia?
Dozens of small models (previous bytes, words, markup, long matches, a small LSTM network) each predict the next bit; learned mixers combine them and an arithmetic coder writes the result.
statico: How far does a grammar compressor (repeated strings become numbered rules) get on text and binaries?
A suffix array finds repeated strings, the best become rules (recursively), and the rule numbers are coded by frequency class and index.
